title: LabelDP-Pro: Learning with Label Differential Privacy via Projections
task_novelty_note: LabelDP training is well-established since Chaudhuri & Hsu (2011); the paper contributes a new method for this existing task.

builds_on.title: Deep learning with differential privacy
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'our approach is built upon it' referring to DP-SGD, and 'we study LabelDP-Pro, a family of methods that tailor DP-SGD to unlock better utility in the high-privacy regime by applying projection operations'

builds_on.title: Deep learning with label differential privacy
builds_on.evidence: Paper states that LP-Normal-SGD from this work 'involves projecting noisy gradients onto a subspace to improve noise scaling. This algorithm is captured by our LabelDP-Pro family' and that it 'has not been developed into a practical one'

compares_to.title: Randomized response: A survey technique for eliminating evasive answer bias
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Tables 5, 6, and 7 as baseline 'RR' with accuracy/AUC numbers alongside LabelDP-Pro

compares_to.title: Deep learning with label differential privacy
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Tables 5 and 6 as baselines 'RR-Debiased', 'LP-2ST', and 'RRWithPrior' with accuracy numbers alongside LabelDP-Pro

compares_to.title: Antipodes of label differential privacy: PATE and ALIBI
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Tables 5 and 6 as baselines 'ALIBI' and 'PATE-FM' with accuracy numbers alongside LabelDP-Pro

compares_to.title: Deep learning with differential privacy
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Tables 5, 6, and 7 as baseline 'DP-SGD' with accuracy/AUC numbers alongside LabelDP-Pro

key_contribution: LabelDP-Pro, a family of label differential privacy training algorithms that project noisy DP-SGD gradients onto convex hulls of per-example per-class gradients computed from public features, achieving the first practical combination of central DP, approximate DP, and LabelDP with privacy amplification by subsampling, and substantially outperforming randomized-response baselines in the high-privacy regime (ε < 1).
limitations: The projection computation requires approximately 200 iterations to converge, introducing a 1.1×–3.8× computational overhead over DP-SGD. The theoretical analysis is restricted to convex loss functions, and the method has only been evaluated on classification tasks, with extension to regression and semi-supervised pipelines left for future work.
surprise_factor: The magnitude of the gap in the high-privacy regime is striking (92.9% vs ~10% on MNIST at ε=0.2), but this is well-predicted by the theoretical noise-scaling analysis (linear vs. exponential in 1/ε), so it is more a confirmation than a surprise. A more genuinely surprising observation is that RR combined with SelfSL produces accuracy *below* random guessing (2.5% at ε=0.01 on CIFAR-10), which the authors trace to the model learning to predict the *wrong* class with high confidence under extreme label noise.

title: Implicit Maximum A Posteriori Filtering via Adaptive Optimization

builds_on.title: The Kalman filter as a special case of the Gauss-Newton method
builds_on.evidence: Paper explicitly uses Theorem 3.1 and Theorem 3.2 of Santos (1996) to establish the equivalence between Kalman filtering and K steps of truncated gradient descent, which is the core theoretical foundation of the IMAP framework.

compares_to.title: Applied optimal estimation
compares_to.evidence: EKF and IEKF listed in Tables 1 and 2 as comparison baselines with RMSE values; paper cites Gelb (1974) for the EKF/IEKF formulation.

compares_to.title: New approach to nonlinear/non-Gaussian Bayesian state estimation
compares_to.evidence: UKF listed in Tables 1 and 2 as comparison baseline with RMSE values; paper cites Julier et al. (1995) for the unscented Kalman filter.

compares_to.title: Sequential Monte Carlo methods in practice
compares_to.evidence: Particle Filter (PF, n=1000) listed in Tables 1, 2, and 3 as comparison baseline with RMSE and accuracy values; paper cites Doucet et al. (2001) for the particle filter.

compares_to.title: The variational Kalman filter and an efficient implementation using limited memory BFGS
compares_to.venue: International Journal for Numerical Methods in Fluids 2010
compares_to.evidence: Variational Kalman Filter (VKF) listed in Table 3 as comparison baseline with classification accuracy values; paper cites Auvinen et al. (2010) for variational Kalman filtering.

key_contribution: Reformulation of Bayesian filtering as optimization over a time-varying objective, showing that adaptive optimizers (e.g., Adam, RMSprop) with K steps implicitly define equivalent filtering priors, and demonstrating that this Implicit MAP Filter matches or outperforms classical filters (EKF, UKF, PF, VKF) while scaling to 28K-parameter neural network weight spaces.
limitations: The framework produces only point estimates (MAP) without full posterior uncertainty, which the authors note limits use in risk-sensitive environments or situations where filtering equations are needed for analysis. The high-dimensional evaluation is limited to a single dataset (Yearbook) with grid-searched hyperparameters, and the particle filter still outperforms IMAP on the low-dimensional toy nonlinear system.
surprise_factor: The conceptual reframing is elegant but not deeply surprising given Santos (1996) and Aitchison (2020); the more notable empirical finding is that a simple Adam optimizer with 50 steps and 3 hyperparameters outperforms a Variational Kalman Filter and a 1000-particle Particle Filter on a 28K-parameter CNN adaptation task, suggesting that the structured inductive biases of classical filters are not necessary when the state space is large and dynamics are unknown. However, the evidence is limited to a single high-dimensional experiment with grid-searched hyperparameters, and the particle filter still wins on the toy nonlinear system, tempering the generality of the claim.

title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Linear Prediction as a Perceptual Metric

builds_on.title: GLICBAWLS - Grey Level Image Compression by Adaptive Weighted Least Squares
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'We make use of a sub-component of the lossless compression algorithm available in Meyer & Tischer (2001) to define a distance between images' and the WLS formulation in Equation (1) is directly derived from this compression algorithm

compares_to.title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Deep Features as a Perceptual Metric
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 1 as supervised baseline (LPIPS) and unsupervised variant (LPIPS fts only) with scores across all BAPPS-2AFC and BAPPS-JND categories; also used in MAD competition in Section 5.3

compares_to.title: An Unsupervised Information-Theoretic Perceptual Quality Metric
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 1 as unsupervised baseline (PIM) with scores across all BAPPS-2AFC and BAPPS-JND categories

compares_to.title: Multiscale Structural Similarity for Image Quality Assessment
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 1 as data-free baseline (MS-SSIM) with scores across all BAPPS-2AFC and BAPPS-JND categories

compares_to.title: From Distance to Dependency: A Paradigm Shift of Full-Reference Image Quality Assessment
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 1 as unsupervised baseline (A-DISTS) with scores on BAPPS-2AFC categories (SRes, Deblur, Color, Interp)

key_contribution: Demonstrates that solving a weighted least squares pixel-prediction problem at inference time (no training data, no neural network) yields perceptual embeddings (LASI) that perform within ~5.8% of the best unsupervised deep-feature methods on BAPPS psychophysical benchmarks, while outperforming hand-crafted MS-SSIM by up to 54%.
limitations: Evaluation is confined to 64×64×3 patches on the single BAPPS dataset, and the authors explicitly note it is unclear whether BAPPS performance generalizes to other tasks or full-resolution images. The method scales cubically with neighborhood size (O(N³) per pixel), and the MAD competition showing complementary failure modes with LPIPS is purely qualitative, with the combination left as future work.
surprise_factor: The conceptual surprise is genuine: a simple linear regression solved at inference time, with no training, no data, and no neural network, closes most of the gap to deep learned perceptual metrics on BAPPS. This is a negative-result surprise against the field's assumption that deep features are required. However, the practical margins are modest (worst-case 5.8% below best unsupervised), evaluation is confined to one dataset of small patches, and the MAD competition is purely qualitative, so the evidence does not yet support a strong claim of paradigm shift.

title: Batch Calibration: Rethinking Calibration for In-Context Learning and Prompt Engineering
task_novelty_note: Calibration of LLM predictions for ICL is well established (CC, DC, PC); the paper contributes a new method for this accepted task.

builds_on.title: Calibrate before use: Improving few-shot performance of language models
builds_on.evidence: BC uses the same affine calibration framework (Wp+b) as CC, with the paper stating it 'unifies various prior approaches' and adopts the linear decision boundary form while changing how the contextual prior is estimated

builds_on.title: Mitigating label biases for in-context learning
builds_on.evidence: BC uses the identical mathematical form W=I, b=-prior as DC, and the paper explicitly states 'instead of relying on content-free tokens, we propose to estimate the contextual bias... from a batch', directly modifying DC's prior estimation

compares_to.title: Calibrate before use: Improving few-shot performance of language models
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 2 as CC baseline with accuracy numbers across all 13 NLP tasks on both PaLM 2-S and PaLM 2-L

compares_to.title: Mitigating label biases for in-context learning
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 2 as DC baseline with accuracy numbers across all 13 NLP tasks on both PaLM 2-S and PaLM 2-L

compares_to.title: Prototypical calibration for few-shot learning of language models
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 2 as PC baseline with accuracy numbers across all 13 NLP tasks on both PaLM 2-S and PaLM 2-L

key_contribution: Proposes Batch Calibration (BC), a zero-shot, inference-only calibration method that estimates contextual bias by marginalizing LLM output scores over a batch of test samples, achieving state-of-the-art performance across 13 NLP classification tasks and zero-shot CLIP image classification with negligible computational overhead.
limitations: BC requires a batch of unlabeled test samples to estimate the contextual bias, which may be impractical in streaming or single-sample settings; the authors note that extending BC to generative tasks and more model modalities remains future work.
surprise_factor: The most notable finding is conceptual: the standard 'content-free token' approach (CC, DC) can actively worsen calibration in multi-sentence tasks because tokens like 'N/A' create spurious surface-level entailment signals, a failure mode not anticipated by prior work. The practical surprise is that a trivial batch mean over test outputs outperforms the more sophisticated GMM-based PC by a wide margin (e.g., 82.45 vs. 69.82 on QNLI with PaLM 2-S), suggesting the added complexity of non-linear boundaries is counterproductive.

title: LLM Augmented LLMs: Expanding Capabilities Through Composition
task_novelty_note: Extends model composition from merging/routing/ensembling to frozen-weight cross-attention composition enabling a joint capability absent from either model.

builds_on.title: Flamingo: a Visual Language Model for Few-Shot Learning
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'they introduce cross-attention parameters across a language model in order to attend to representations from an image encoder... In this work, we extend the ideology of model re-use and modularity to composition of capabilities in large language models' — adapting the cross-attention composition pattern between two frozen models from multi-modal to LLM-LLM setting.

builds_on.title: LegoNN: Building Modular Encoder-Decoder Models
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'The modular encoder-decoder based method in Dalmia et al. (2022) adapts components of encoder-decoder models to allow flexible re-usability of different encoders, each with their own capabilities. In this work, we extend the ideology of model re-use and modularity to composition of capabilities in large language models.'

compares_to.title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 5 as a direct comparison baseline with numerical results across FLORES-200, GSM-8K, CC, T2C, and C2T metrics; Section 4.4 states 'we evaluate a parameter efficient fine-tuning approach by training LoRA layers to adapt m_B' with matched parameter count.

key_contribution: Proposes CALM, a framework that composes two frozen LLMs via learned cross-attention over their intermediate layer representations, enabling new joint capabilities (e.g., low-resource translation, code generation) that neither model possesses alone, using only 5–20% of domain data while preserving the anchor model's existing capabilities and matching or exceeding fully fine-tuned baselines.
limitations: All experiments are conducted within the PaLM2 architecture family at small-to-medium scale (XXS/XS/S), so generalizability to heterogeneous architectures or much larger models is untested. Composition with multiple augmenting models simultaneously is identified as future work rather than evaluated.
surprise_factor: The most notable finding is that CALM matches or exceeds fully fine-tuned baselines (mB^NTL, mB^Code) while using only 5–7% of the training data and preserving the anchor model's existing capabilities, suggesting that the cross-attention bottleneck is a surprisingly effective interface for capability transfer. However, the evidence is confined to the PaLM2 architecture family at small-to-medium scale, which limits confidence in the generality of these results.

title: SEA: Sparse Linear Attention with Estimated Attention Mask

builds_on.title: Rethinking Attention with Performers
builds_on.evidence: SEA directly uses Performer (FAVOR+) as its kernel-based linear attention estimator: 'we decode the output features of the kernel-based linear attention method Performer (Choromanski et al., 2021) to form Â'

builds_on.title: TinyBERT: Distilling BERT for Natural Language Understanding
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'Our training scheme is similar to previous transformer KD work (Jiao et al., 2020) since we approximate the context features and attention matrices' and extends it with an additional attention matrix matching loss

compares_to.title: Reformer: The Efficient Transformer
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 2 (Wikitext2), Table A.8 (MNLI), and Tables A.1/A.2 (efficiency) with perplexity, accuracy, memory, and latency numbers alongside SEA

compares_to.title: Rethinking Attention with Performers
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 2 (Wikitext2), Table A.8 (MNLI), Tables A.1/A.2 (efficiency), Table A.5 (longer context), and Table A.7 (OpenWebText) with perplexity, accuracy, memory, and latency numbers

compares_to.title: CosFormer: Rethinking Softmax in Attention
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table A.8 (MNLI) and Tables A.1/A.2 (efficiency) with accuracy, memory, and latency numbers alongside SEA

compares_to.title: Sparse Sinkhorn Attention
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table A.8 (MNLI) and Tables A.1/A.2 (efficiency) with accuracy, memory, and latency numbers alongside SEA

compares_to.title: Synthesizer: Rethinking Self-Attention in Transformer Models
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table A.8 (MNLI) and Tables A.1/A.2 (efficiency) with accuracy, memory, and latency numbers alongside SEA

compares_to.title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Tables A.1/A.2 (efficiency benchmarks) with memory and latency numbers alongside SEA at various sequence lengths

key_contribution: Proposes SEA, a linear-complexity attention mechanism that estimates a compressed attention matrix via Performer and a CNN decoder, applies grouped top-k selection to generate a sparse mask, and performs sparse attention, enabling knowledge distillation from a pretrained quadratic teacher while matching or slightly exceeding the quadratic baseline (OPT-1.3B: 13.5 vs. 13.9 PPL) with ~55% less memory.
limitations: The authors note that the uniform interpolation used to expand the compressed mask to full size is suboptimal (it does not account for attention probability distribution) and that a learnable masking method (e.g., concrete masking) or non-uniform/learnable interpolation could further improve performance. Evaluation is limited to models up to OPT-1.3B with only 10k training steps, and SEA incurs higher latency than pure linear methods (e.g., Performer) due to the dual kernel+sparse attention path.
surprise_factor: The most notable result is that SEA slightly outperforms the vanilla quadratic OPT-1.3B baseline (13.5 vs. 13.9 PPL) while using ~55% less memory, and that increasing k after training further widens this gap — a linear method beating its quadratic teacher is counterintuitive. However, the margin is small, the training budget is limited (10k steps), and the comparison is on a single dataset, so the effect's robustness at scale is unproven. The 47.7% perplexity gap over Performer is large but Performer is a known weak baseline for causal LM.

title: Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
task_novelty_note: Extends sycophancy evaluation from multiple-choice research-model settings (Perez et al., 2022) to free-form production assistants and adds causal analysis of the RLHF training pipeline.

builds_on.title: Discovering language model behaviors with model-written evaluations
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'We use both human-written and model-written evaluations (Perez et al., 2022)' and extends their sycophancy evaluation framework to production AI assistants and new free-form tasks.

compares_to.title: Training a helpful and harmless assistant with reinforcement learning from human feedback
compares_to.evidence: The 52B parameter preference model from this work is compared against the paper's Bayesian logistic regression model (71.3% vs ~72% holdout accuracy in §4.1) and against the Claude 2 PM for sycophancy during RL training (Appendix C.2, Fig. 21).

key_contribution: Demonstrates that sycophancy is a consistent behavior across five production AI assistants (Claude 1.3/2.0, GPT-3.5/4, LLaMA-2-70B) via a four-task free-form benchmark (SycophancyEval), and provides causal evidence that human preference data incentivizes sycophantic responses by showing that matching user beliefs is among the most predictive features of human preference judgments in hh-rlhf and that the Claude 2 preference model prefers convincingly-written sycophantic responses over truthful ones a non-negligible fraction of the time.
limitations: The 266-misconception dataset is explicitly described as an initial proof-of-concept requiring a larger dataset with more comprehensive fact-verification for definitive evaluation, and the crowd-workers judging sycophancy are not the users who hold the misconception (mimicking a sandwiching setting with no internet access). The PM optimization experiments are limited to the Claude 2 preference model, and the authors note that pretraining and supervised finetuning also likely contribute to sycophancy, so the causal attribution to human feedback is partial rather than exclusive.
surprise_factor: The most conceptually striking finding is that the Claude 2 PM prefers sycophantic responses over even helpful truthful ones ~45% of the time on the hardest misconceptions, and that independent human crowd-workers show a similar (if smaller) bias—suggesting the problem is partly baked into human judgment itself, not just model optimization. The 98% wrong-admission rate for Claude 1.3 when challenged is also notably extreme. However, the 95% PM preference for sycophantic over baseline truthful is somewhat expected given the baseline is a terse 5-word correction versus a full persuasive paragraph, so the more meaningful comparison is the helpful-truthful vs. sycophantic gap.

title: Entropy Coding of Unordered Data Structures
task_novelty_note: Extends unordered-data compression from specific types (multisets, simple graphs) to all permutable classes via a unified coset-based codec.

builds_on.title: Practical Lossless Compression with Latent Variables Using Bits Back Coding
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'we can use the bits-back with ANS method introduced by Townsend et al. (2019), the key idea being to decode an ordering as part of an encode function' — this is the core mechanism for achieving the discount term.

builds_on.title: Compressing Multisets with Large Alphabets
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'Our method can be viewed as a generalization of the framework for multiset compression presented in Severo et al. (2023a), which also used bits-back with ANS' — shuffle coding directly generalizes their multiset-specific approach to arbitrary unordered objects.

compares_to.title: Partition and Code: Learning How to Compress Graphs
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 3 as 'PnC' with bits-per-edge numbers alongside shuffle coding results for MUTAG, PTC_MR, ZINC_full, PROTEINS, IMDB-BINARY, and IMDB-MULTI datasets.

compares_to.title: Compression of Graphical Structures: Fundamental Limits, Algorithms, and Experiments
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 3 (lower section) as 'SZIP' with bits-per-edge numbers alongside shuffle coding net rate for Airports, Protein interaction, Collaboration, Genetic interaction, and Internet datasets.

key_contribution: Shuffle coding, a general model-agnostic method for optimal lossless compression of sequences of unordered objects (graphs, multisets, hypergraphs) that achieves the information-theoretic rate by subtracting a log(n!/|Aut(f)|) discount from any ordered-object codec via bits-back coding over automorphism-group cosets, demonstrating 26–47% compression gains on real graph datasets.
limitations: Canonical ordering and automorphism group computation have no known polynomial-time algorithm for general graphs, making worst-case runtime impractical. The method achieves optimal rate only for sequences of objects; the one-shot case incurs an O(log n!) initial-bit overhead that is not amortized.
surprise_factor: The most notable finding is that a simple, non-neural method with basic statistical models (ER, Pólya urn) matches or beats the neural PnC method on several datasets (e.g., 1.82 vs 1.99 bits/edge on ZINC_full, 1.14 vs 0.38 on IMDB-MULTI where PnC wins), suggesting that the structural discount from removing ordering information is a larger lever than model sophistication for these graph sizes. The 26–47% discount is large but largely predictable from the log(n!) term, so the conceptual surprise is modest.

title: NEMESIS: Normalizing the Soft-Prompt Vectors of Vision-Language Models
task_novelty_note: Few-shot image classification with prompt-tuned VLMs is well established; the contribution is a new normalization loss and empirical discovery about prompt norms, not a new task formulation.

builds_on.title: Learning to prompt for vision-language models
builds_on.evidence: The paper states 'we train the CoOp model and obtain the learned prompt vectors' and Nemesis is described as a normalization loss 'easily integrated into existing soft-prompt methods' with the main algorithm (Algorithm 1) directly extending CoOp's training loop.

compares_to.title: Learning to prompt for vision-language models
compares_to.evidence: CoOp is the primary baseline compared against in Table 1 (domain generalization), Table 3 (ablation), Table 4 (beta ablation), Table A5 (few-shot on 11 datasets), and Figure 2 (few-shot recognition curves).

compares_to.title: Plot: Prompt learning with optimal transport for vision-language models
compares_to.evidence: PLOT is compared against in Table 2 (few-shot recognition on Caltech101, DTD, Flowers102) and in Table A8 (computation cost analysis) as an ensemble-based prompt-tuning baseline.

compares_to.title: Conditional prompt learning for vision-language models
compares_to.evidence: CoCoOp is the baseline in Table A4 (base-to-new generalization setting) where CoCoOp+Nemesis variants are compared against CoCoOp across 11 datasets.

key_contribution: First systematic investigation of soft-prompt vector norms in vision-language models, uncovering the Low-Norm Effect (reducing norms at specific positions improves performance) and proposing the Nemesis method with Position-Uniform and Position-Aware Normalization losses that improve CoOp by up to 4% on few-shot classification across 11 datasets.
limitations: The Low-Norm Effect is highly dataset-dependent (absent on Flowers102 and SUN397 in many settings), the mechanistic explanation remains speculative, and the PAN loss introduces up to 4× computational overhead that scales with the number of corruption positions. The authors note that determining the optimal normalization strength ω per dataset and mitigating the computational burden of PAN remain open problems.
surprise_factor: The conceptual surprise is moderate: the field had focused entirely on prompt content and alignment, yet the mere magnitude of prompt vectors at specific positions turns out to be a meaningful performance lever, with reducing norms helping and increasing them hurting. However, the effect is inconsistent across datasets, the explanation is post-hoc, and the practical gains (1–4%) are modest, so this is an interesting observation rather than a field-shifting result.

title: What Does the Knowledge Neuron Thesis Have to Do with Knowledge?
task_novelty_note: Extends model-editing evaluation from factual cloze tasks to syntactic minimal pairs and adds symmetry/synonymy criteria beyond prior reliability/generality/locality metrics.

builds_on.title: Knowledge Neurons in Pretrained Transformers
builds_on.evidence: Paper directly adopts and extends the KN search algorithm (integral of gradients) to localise syntactic phenomena, stating 'we follow Dai et al. (2022) and use the integral of gradients to calculate the neuron attribution score'

builds_on.title: Locating and editing factual associations in GPT
builds_on.evidence: Paper directly uses ROME model editing and causal tracing methodology, stating 'we reassess Meng et al.'s (2022) similar but more intricate implementation of KN edit' and reproduces their causal tracing on syntactic phenomena

builds_on.title: Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Are Key-Value Memories
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'Geva et al. (2021) were among the first to propose that the MLP modules in a transformer model behave like key-value memories' and the entire KN thesis being evaluated derives from this interpretation

compares_to.title: Knowledge Neurons in Pretrained Transformers
compares_to.evidence: KN edit reliability scores (1.66%–47.86%) are presented in Figure 6c alongside ROME results, and KN edit is applied to syntactic phenomena in Section 3 for direct comparison with ROME

compares_to.title: Locating and editing factual associations in GPT
compares_to.evidence: ROME is evaluated under the paper's new symmetry and synonymy criteria in Table 1, with reliability scores of 96–100% but symmetry/synonym scores of only 23–58%

compares_to.title: Editing Large Language Models: Problems, Methods, and Opportunities
compares_to.evidence: Paper extends Yao et al.'s portability evaluation framework with two new criteria (bijective symmetry and synonymous invariance), and cites their KN edit reliability results in Figure 6c

key_contribution: Demonstrates that the Knowledge Neuron Thesis is an oversimplification by showing that syntactic phenomena (determiner-noun, subject-verb agreement) localise to MLP neurons with the same metrics and layer distribution as factual information, and that KN-inspired editing methods (KN edit, ROME) fail under two new evaluation criteria—bijective symmetry and synonymous invariance—suggesting MLP neurons store 'token expression patterns' rather than knowledge.
limitations: The evaluation is limited to English agreement phenomena (determiner-noun, subject-verb, anaphor) on relatively small models (BERT-base, GPT-2 base/XL, LLaMA-2 7B), and the authors note that the effect of individual-neuron editing becomes less pronounced on larger models. The paper also acknowledges that circuit-level interpretation methods are currently 'ad hoc' and 'have only been applied to a small set of tasks,' and it does not run its own experiments on CounterFact and ZsRE, instead citing prior results.
surprise_factor: The most notable finding is conceptual: syntactic phenomena (determiner-noun, subject-verb agreement) localise to MLP neurons with the same metrics, same topmost-layer distribution, and same editing limitations as factual information, suggesting no mechanistic divide between 'formal' and 'functional' competence. This is a well-evidenced negative result (multiple models, paradigms, statistical tests) that challenges the working assumption that facts and grammar are processed by distinct circuits, though the individual reliability numbers (5.2% categorical overturn for syntax, 23–33% symmetry for ROME) are not shocking in isolation.

title: Robust NAS under Adversarial Training: Benchmark, Theory, and Beyond
task_novelty_note: Robust NAS is an established task (Guo et al. 2020, Mok et al. 2021); the paper contributes a new adversarially-trained benchmark and multi-objective NTK theory for it.

builds_on.title: NAS-Bench-201: Extending the scope of reproducible neural architecture search
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'We construct our benchmark based on a commonly-used cell-based search space in the NAS community: NAS-Bench-201 (Dong & Yang, 2020), which consists of 6 edges and 5 operators'

builds_on.title: Neural tangent kernel: Convergence and generalization in neural networks
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'leveraging the neural tangent kernel (NTK) tool from deep learning theory, we establish a generalization theory for searching architecture in terms of clean accuracy and robust accuracy under multi-objective adversarial training'

builds_on.title: Generalization properties of NAS under activation and skip connection search
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'Prior literature (Oymak et al., 2021; Zhu et al., 2022a) establishes the generalization guarantee of the searched architecture under standard training based on neural tangent kernel (NTK)' and extends this to adversarial training

builds_on.title: Generalization bounds of stochastic gradient descent for wide and deep neural networks
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'the generalization guarantee of over-parameterized FCNN under standard training has been established in Cao & Gu (2019); Zhu et al. (2022a)' and extends to multi-objective adversarial training

compares_to.title: Regularized evolution for image classifier architecture search
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 2 as a NAS algorithm baseline with clean and robust accuracy numbers across multiple attack schemes

compares_to.title: Random search and reproducibility for neural architecture search
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 2 as a NAS algorithm baseline with clean and robust accuracy numbers across multiple attack schemes

compares_to.title: Exploring the loss landscape in neural architecture search
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 2 as a NAS algorithm baseline (Local Search) with clean and robust accuracy numbers across multiple attack schemes

compares_to.title: Neural architecture design and robustness: A dataset
compares_to.evidence: Compared in Table 1 via Spearman rank correlation coefficients between NAS-RobBench-201 and the Jung et al. benchmark for clean, PGD, and FGSM accuracies

key_contribution: Releases NAS-RobBench-201, the first adversarially-trained NAS benchmark covering 6,466 architectures on three datasets (~107k GPU hours), and establishes NTK-based generalization bounds for multi-objective adversarial training showing that clean accuracy is governed by a joint clean-robust NTK while robust accuracy is governed by a robust NTK and its twice-perturbed version.
limitations: The benchmark and theoretical results do not explore vision Transformers, and the NTK-based analysis is confined to the linear (infinite-width) regime, which cannot fully explain the success of neural networks in practice.
surprise_factor: The most notable empirical finding is the low Spearman correlation (0.382) between PGD robust accuracy under adversarial training and under standard training (Table 1), demonstrating that architecture rankings for robustness are substantially reshaped by the training procedure — a practical surprise that undermines the use of existing standard-trained benchmarks for robust NAS. The theoretical decomposition into joint NTKs is a clean conceptual contribution but not deeply surprising given the structure of the multi-objective loss.

title: Dynamic Sparse No Training: Training-Free Fine-Tuning for Sparse LLMs
task_novelty_note: Pruning and fine-tuning LLMs is well-established; DSOT introduces a training-free method for the already-accepted fine-tuning sub-task.

builds_on.title: Scalable training of artificial neural networks with adaptive sparse connectivity inspired by network science
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'we isolate pruning-and-growing from network training, and formulate it as an iterative approach to progressively optimize sparse masks' — directly adapting DST's pruning-and-growing mechanism to a training-free setting

builds_on.title: A simple and effective pruning approach for large language models

Evaluation is limited to perplexity and zero-shot accuracy on LLaMA/Vicuna/OPT families, with no assessment of generation quality, instruction-following, or composition with quantization.

key_contribution: MIRAGE, a model-agnostic graph distillation algorithm that mines frequently co-occurring computation trees from message-passing GNNs using FP-Growth, achieving 4–5× better compression and 150× faster distillation than gradient-matching baselines (DOSCOND, KIDD) while maintaining competitive AUC-ROC across GCN, GAT, and GIN architectures.
limitations: MIRAGE relies on the assumption that the computation-tree frequency distribution is skewed (power-law), which may not hold for heterophilous datasets. Its applicability to graph transformers, equivariant GNNs, and temporal graphs remains unexplored, and it cannot generalize to unseen tasks.
surprise_factor: The conceptual surprise is that gradient information is entirely unnecessary for effective graph distillation — the power-law structure of computation trees alone suffices to achieve competitive accuracy with 4–5× better compression. The 150× speedup is impressive but largely explained by the absence of iterative gradient optimization and GPU dependency. Accuracy gains are modest (top-2 rather than consistently #1), so the practical surprise is more about efficiency and robustness than predictive performance.

key_contribution: Introduces the Influencer Backdoor Attack (IBA) on semantic segmentation, where a small natural trigger placed on non-victim pixels indirectly causes misclassification of all victim-class pixels, and proposes Nearest Neighbor Injection and Pixel Random Labeling techniques that achieve >90% attack success rate with only 5% poisoning while making the attack robust to arbitrary trigger-victim distances.
limitations: The defense evaluation is limited to two intuitive methods (fine-tuning and pruning), and it remains unclear how to adapt more sophisticated backdoor defenses to segmentation. The authors acknowledge that the methodology may encounter challenges in more complex, variable real-world scenarios beyond the controlled outdoor settings tested, and future research should explore broader real-world conditions to enhance generalizability.
surprise_factor: The PRL result is moderately surprising: randomly relabeling ~50k pixels to other classes present in the same image substantially boosts ASR and, more notably, makes the attack nearly distance-invariant (ASR stays above 90% from 0–60 to 120–150 px trigger-victim distance), whereas NNI collapses to ~45% at the same far distance. The mechanism—forcing the model to aggregate broader context to minimize loss on randomly corrupted labels—makes the model more susceptible to a distant trigger, which is a non-obvious interaction between label noise and attention/context in segmentation networks.

title: A Newborn Embodied Turing Test for Comparing Object Segmentation Across Animals and Machines
task_novelty_note: Object segmentation is a well-established CV task; the paper's contribution is a new matched-experience embodied benchmark for evaluating it under one-shot, single-object-on-single-background conditions.

builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'We focused on the object segmentation/recognition task and behavioral data from (Wood & Wood, 2021) (Exp.1)' and creates digital twins of that experiment's environments

builds_on.evidence: Prior NETT for a different task (view-invariant recognition); this paper extends the NETT framework to object segmentation, citing it as a precedent for the digital twin design

key_contribution: Introduces the Newborn Embodied Turing Test (NETT) for object segmentation, a matched-experience digital-twin benchmark in which newborn chicks and artificial agents are raised in identical environments and tested on identical tasks, demonstrating that all 35 chicks solved one-shot background-invariant object recognition while none of the tested ML algorithms (spanning CNNs, ResNets, LSTMs, DVS sensors, 10× training, and pre-trained encoders including SAM, DINOv2, and Ego4D) could, exposing a fundamental gap between statistical learning and biological visual development.
limitations: The paper tested a limited number of ANN architectures and used lower-dimensional action spaces to avoid high-dimensional control challenges; additionally, artificial agents had a single imprinting objective rather than the multiple homeostatic needs (hunger, thirst, curiosity) that shape learning in real chicks.
surprise_factor: The negative result is genuinely surprising: even 86M-parameter SAM (trained on 1B+ annotations) and DINOv2, which excel on standard segmentation benchmarks, still learned background-dependent representations and failed the one-shot task that chicks solve effortlessly. The consistency of failure across all six architectural variants (encoder size, recurrence, dynamic sensing, training duration, pre-training) strengthens the claim that this is a fundamental algorithmic limitation rather than an implementation artifact, though the evidence is confined to PPO-based embodied agents in a single virtual environment.

surprise_factor: The 200× parameter reduction (53K vs ~10M TCN) for matching a detailed biophysical neuron's spike-level I/O is a genuinely striking result, well-supported by ablations showing that ~20 memory units with ~25ms timescales and nonlinear MLP integration are the critical components. The conceptual surprise is that a single simple recurrent cell with constant explicit timescales can rival or beat much more complex architectures (Transformers, Chrono-LSTM) on long-range tasks, challenging the assumption that multi-layered processing is necessary for long-horizon dependencies.

limitations: The choice of the unbalancedness parameter τ requires a grid search and its optimal value is application-dependent, with no principled selection criterion. All experiments use the squared Euclidean distance as cost, and the authors note that exploring geometry-aware costs tailored to the underlying data space is a future direction.
surprise_factor: The most striking result is the Ngn3 EP cell transition improvement from 7% to 69% in single-cell trajectory inference, where the balanced OT-ICNN produces biologically implausible mappings due to proliferation-driven distribution shift. The elegance of a single re-scaling step working universally across three architecturally distinct estimators (ICNN, Monge Gap, Flow Matching) is also notable, though the overall performance gains in image translation are moderate and consistent with the expected benefit of handling class imbalance.

surprise_factor: The most notable finding is the robustness gap under decreasing expert coverage: GoFAR's performance collapses (36% drop at 1% expert data) while SMORe degrades gracefully (16% drop), validating the discriminator-free design choice in a way that is not immediately obvious from the theory alone. The consistent outperformance across 12+ diverse tasks (manipulation, dexterous hand, locomotion) with a single set of hyperparameters (β=0.5) is also somewhat impressive, though the theoretical grounding makes the direction of improvement predictable.

limitations: Evaluation is confined to relatively small, clean-domain datasets (ATIS, WSJ) and a single small ASR model (Whisper-tiny), leaving open whether gains persist with larger LLMs, larger ASR backbones, or in streaming/real-time settings. The paper notes in Appendix A.5 that removing the N-best list and relying solely on acoustic tokens as prefix is unresolved, and the AVSR extension is limited to LRS3 with a specific pre-trained lip-reading model and a small number of SNR conditions.
surprise_factor: The most notable finding is that early fusion with speech tokens actually degrades performance below the text-only GER baseline, providing a concrete, quantified demonstration of modality laziness in the LLM-ASR context. Additionally, the calibration visualization revealing that 98.9% of LLM token predictions cluster in the 0.9–1.0 confidence interval (with 99.9% average confidence vs. 96.5% true accuracy) is a striking illustration of over-confidence in auto-regressive decoding. However, the evidence is limited to small datasets and a Whisper-tiny ASR model, tempering the generality of these observations.

title: Rethinking Information-Theoretic Generalization: Loss Entropy Induced PAC Bounds
task_novelty_note: Generalization error bounding is a well-established task; the paper introduces a new loss-entropy-based method for it.

builds_on.title: How does information bottleneck help deep learning?
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'We demonstrate that the recently established bounds by Kawaguchi et al. (2023) can be further enhanced by substituting the mutual information between input and representation with loss entropy'

builds_on.title: A new family of generalization bounds using samplewise evaluated cmi
builds_on.evidence: Paper extends the supersample CMI framework by replacing multivariate mutual information I(R̃^W;Ũ|S̃_s) with loss entropy H(R̃_Δ^W), and alleviates the bounded loss assumption

builds_on.title: Tighter information-theoretic generalization bounds from supersamples
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'This concept was first explored in (Wang & Mao, 2023)' regarding loss differences, and extends it to loss entropy metrics via concavity of Shannon's entropy

builds_on.title: Reasoning about generalization via conditional mutual information
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'The supersample framework was initially explored by Steinke & Zakynthinou (2020) for generalization analysis' and builds the supersample setting (Theorem 4) on this framework

builds_on.title: On leave-one-out conditional mutual information for generalization
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'The leave-one-out (LOO) setting was recently introduced by Rammal et al. (2022) for generalization analysis' and derives Theorem 3 in this setting

compares_to.title: A new family of generalization bounds using samplewise evaluated cmi
compares_to.evidence: Figure 2 directly compares the proposed Square-Root (Theorem 4) and Fast-Rate (Theorem 6) bounds against the Binary KL bound (Theorem 7 in Hellström & Durisi, 2022) across MNIST-Adam, CIFAR10-SGD, and MNIST-SGLD scenarios

compares_to.title: How does information bottleneck help deep learning?
compares_to.evidence: Figure 1 compares Pearson correlation of H(L^w) and H(L^w|Y) against I(X;T^w) and I(X;T^w|Y) from Kawaguchi et al. (2023) as metrics for predicting generalization error on synthetic 2D Gaussian datasets

key_contribution: A family of computationally tractable PAC generalization bounds expressed in terms of one-dimensional loss entropies (Shannon and Rényi) that replace high-dimensional mutual information terms, combined with a thresholding strategy that alleviates the bounded loss assumption for long-tailed distributions such as cross-entropy.
limitations: The data-independent bounds (Theorems 1–2) require the model to be fixed and independent of the training dataset, limiting their direct applicability to standard supervised training; the threshold κ in Theorem 6 is manually set rather than chosen adaptively. The empirical evaluation is confined to relatively simple tasks (synthetic 2D Gaussian, binarized MNIST, CIFAR-10) and does not test the bounds on larger-scale or multi-task settings.
surprise_factor: The empirical finding that H(L^w|Y) achieves the highest Pearson correlation (0.635) with generalization error—substantially outperforming I(X;T^w|Y) (0.384) and I(W;S) (0.021)—is a clean validation of the theoretical argument, though it comes from a single synthetic 2D Gaussian setup. The conceptual insight that a 1D loss entropy suffices where high-dimensional mutual information was previously required is elegant but follows naturally from the DPI argument, so it is more a satisfying unification than a genuine surprise.

task_novelty_note: Extends FRL from off-policy (Q-learning, TD(0)) to on-policy (SARSA) with heterogeneous environments and linear function approximation.

builds_on.title: On-line Q-learning using connectionist systems
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'we propose a novel algorithm, FedSARSA, integrating SARSA, a classic on-policy temporal difference (TD) control algorithm (Rummery & Niranjan, 1994; Singh & Sutton, 1996), into a federated learning framework'

builds_on.title: Reinforcement learning with replacing eligibility traces
builds_on.evidence: SARSA algorithm (the core on-policy TD control method) is attributed to both Rummery & Niranjan (1994) and Singh & Sutton (1996); FedSARSA directly extends this to the federated setting

builds_on.title: Communication-efficient learning of deep networks from decentralized data
builds_on.evidence: Paper adopts the server-client federated learning model with periodic aggregation 'akin to well-known algorithms like FedAvg (McMahan et al., 2017)'

builds_on.title: Finite-sample analysis for sarsa with linear function approximation
builds_on.evidence: Paper extends the single-agent finite-time analysis of linear SARSA to the federated setting, stating 'the finite-time analysis for linear SARSA was provided by Zou et al. (2019)' and building on its convergence framework

builds_on.title: Federated temporal difference learning with linear function approximation under environmental heterogeneity
builds_on.evidence: Paper extends federated TD(0) (off-policy) to on-policy SARSA, noting 'Wang et al. (2023a) presented a finite time analysis of federated TD(0) that can handle environmental heterogeneity' and that FedSARSA reduces to federated TD(0) with a fixed policy

key_contribution: First finite-time analysis of an on-policy federated reinforcement learning algorithm (FedSARSA) with linear function approximation under environmental heterogeneity, proving N-fold linear speedup and characterizing the convergence region radius as O(ε_p + ε_r) around each agent's optimal policy.
limitations: The theoretical guarantees require a Lipschitz-continuous policy improvement operator (excluding the standard greedy selector used in Q-learning), linear function approximation (no nonlinear approximators), and full synchronous participation of all agents at every communication round. The analysis also assumes uniform ergodicity with a uniform mixing rate across all agents' MDPs, and simulations are limited to small discrete state-action spaces (|S|=|A|=100).
surprise_factor: The linear speedup result in the on-policy setting is non-trivial: one might expect the time-varying behavior policies to destroy the variance-reduction benefit of averaging across agents, yet the N-fold speedup is preserved. The backtracking technique—virtually freezing the policy for a short window to recover stationarity—is a clever analytical device that makes this possible, though the result itself (linear speedup) aligns with expectations from the federated optimization literature.

builds_on.title: Riemannian conjugate gradient methods: General framework and specific algorithms with convergence analyses
builds_on.evidence: Paper extends the Riemannian conjugate gradient framework to a decentralized setting, replacing vector transports with projection operators while retaining the Fletcher-Reeves beta formula structure

builds_on.title: Decentralized Riemannian gradient descent on the Stiefel manifold
builds_on.evidence: Paper builds on the decentralized Riemannian gradient descent framework over the Stiefel manifold, extending it from steepest descent to conjugate gradient with search direction consensus

builds_on.title: Decentralized projected Riemannian gradient method for smooth optimization on compact submanifolds
builds_on.evidence: Paper adopts the projection-based update strategy (replacing retractions with nearest-point projection) from this work, applying it to the conjugate gradient search direction update

compares_to.title: Decentralized Riemannian gradient descent on the Stiefel manifold
compares_to.evidence: DRDGD is directly compared against DRCGD in Figures 1-4 on both synthetic and MNIST data, with consensus error, gradient norm, objective gap, and distance to optimum metrics

compares_to.title: Decentralized projected Riemannian gradient method for smooth optimization on compact submanifolds
compares_to.evidence: DPRGD is directly compared against DRCGD in Figures 1-4 on both synthetic and MNIST data, with consensus error, gradient norm, objective gap, and distance to optimum metrics

key_contribution: The first decentralized Riemannian conjugate gradient algorithm (DRCGD) on the Stiefel manifold that replaces expensive retractions and vector transports with projection operators, achieving global convergence to a stationary point with O(1/√K) rate while reducing per-agent computational cost.
limitations: The analysis is restricted to the Stiefel manifold rather than general compact submanifolds, and the convergence proof relies on an extended assumption (Eq. 20) bounding the projected consensus direction by the differentiated-retraction transport that is not verified for all practical settings. The authors note future work on extending to compact submanifolds and developing decentralized online optimization over Riemannian manifolds.
surprise_factor: The moderate conceptual surprise is that a simple tangent-space projection suffices to replace the vector transport in the conjugate gradient search direction update while preserving global convergence in the decentralized setting — this was not previously established and suggests the transport structure may be less essential than assumed. Empirically, DRCGD consistently outperforms DRDGD and DPRGD, but the margins are moderate and the evaluation is limited to eigenvector problems on synthetic and MNIST data.

limitations: The model is evaluated on only two datasets (UK Biobank and HCP) and a single imaging modality (fMRI), and zero-shot functional network classification achieves a modest 58.8% accuracy across 7 networks. The authors identify multi-modal integration (EEG, MEG, structural MRI), broader cognitive-state probing, and evaluation on expanded functional atlases as important future directions.
surprise_factor: The most notable finding is the zero-shot functional network recovery (58.8% accuracy) purely from attention weights, which had no network-based supervision during training—this is conceptually interesting but the absolute accuracy is modest. The generalization to the external HCP cohort (R²=0.278) and the consistent scaling with model/data size are expected for foundation models and not particularly surprising. Overall, the results are solid but represent incremental improvements over strong baselines rather than a paradigm-shifting result.

The generator-discriminator architecture and adversarial loss are the foundational algorithmic structure of Branch-GAN.

compares_to.evidence: GPT-4 appears as a strong baseline in Tables 1, 3, 6, and 7 with human evaluation percentages and automatic metrics directly compared against Branch-GAN models.

key_contribution: Branch-GAN introduces a branching self-attention schema that enables parallel generation of multiple short continuations from each training sample, providing dense per-token adversarial reward signals compatible with Transformer parallelism, and demonstrates that this GAN-based fine-tuning with less than 0.01% of pre-training data makes a 410M-parameter model outperform a 6.9B-parameter baseline in human-evaluated text quality.
limitations: Experiments are constrained by limited computational resources: models are at most 1B parameters, training uses only 12.8M tokens (<0.01% of Pile), branching depth is fixed at 16 tokens, and evaluation uses only 100 contexts per domain. The authors explicitly note that the perplexity-quality dissociation may be an artifact of the very small training set and encourage further research on scaling to larger foundation models, more training data, and training without MLE pre-training.
surprise_factor: The 16× parameter efficiency gap (410M Branch-GAN beating 6.9B Pythia in human preference) is the most striking result, though it rests on small models, a single corpus, and 100 contexts per domain, so the margin may not hold at scale. A more conceptually interesting finding is that Branch-GAN models exhibit substantially higher perplexity and NLL on held-out data than baselines while producing text humans prefer, challenging the working assumption that lower perplexity tracks better generation quality — though the authors themselves caution this may be an artifact of their tiny training set.

title: Maximum Entropy Model Correction in Reinforcement Learning
task_novelty_note: Model-based RL with approximate models is a well-studied task; the contribution is a new correction method (MaxEnt MoCo) for this established problem.

builds_on.title: Maximum entropy density estimation with generalized regularization and an application to species distribution modeling
builds_on.evidence: The core MaxEnt MoCo correction procedure is directly derived from this work: 'This procedure is known as Maximum Entropy density estimation (Dudik et al., 2007)' and the regularized formulation (P2) uses the ℓ₂² regularization from this paper.

builds_on.title: Integrated architectures for learning, planning, and reacting based on approximating dynamic programming
builds_on.evidence: The paper explicitly states 'MoCoDyna, which extends the Dyna framework' and MoCoDyna's sample-based loop with model updates and planning iterations directly extends the Dyna architecture.

compares_to.evidence: Figure 1 compares MoCoVI against OS-VI and MoCoDyna against OS-Dyna with normalized error curves across low/medium/high model error settings.

compares_to.title: Integrated architectures for learning, planning, and reacting based on approximating dynamic programming
compares_to.evidence: Figure 1 (bottom) compares MoCoDyna against Dyna, showing 'Dyna cannot solve the task due to the model error' while MoCoDyna succeeds.

key_contribution: A Maximum Entropy Model Correction (MaxEnt MoCo) framework that minimally adjusts an approximate transition model's next-state distributions via KL-divergence-constrained density estimation using a small number of true-dynamics queries, yielding MoCoVI and MoCoDyna algorithms that provably converge to the true value function at a rate strictly faster than model-free value iteration when the model is sufficiently accurate.
limitations: Empirical validation is restricted to a single 6×6 grid world environment, and the authors explicitly note that deep RL applications of the MoCo framework remain unexplored. The method requires costly queries to the true dynamics Pφ at each iteration, and the theoretical guarantees depend on worst-case (ℓ∞) model and query error bounds, which may be pessimistic in practice.
surprise_factor: The conceptual surprise is moderate: the paper shows that correcting the transition kernel (rather than the reward, as in OS-VI) via MaxEnt density estimation yields a strictly better convergence rate γ' < γ and, notably, does not diverge even when γ' > 1, whereas OS-VI can diverge under the same conditions. However, the empirical evidence is confined to a small 6×6 grid world, so the practical magnitude of the improvement in realistic settings remains unvalidated.

title: Does Writing with Language Models Reduce Content Diversity?
task_novelty_note: Extends text diversity measurement (n-gram TTR, self-BLEU) to the interactive co-writing setting, adding attribution of diversity loss to model vs. user contributions.

builds_on.title: Coauthor: Designing a human-ai collaborative writing dataset for exploring language model capabilities
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'We adopt the CoAuthor platform developed by Lee et al. (2022a)' as the experimental infrastructure for data collection, including the TAB-key suggestion interface and keystroke-level logging.

builds_on.title: Locally typical sampling
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'We adapt these metrics for co-writing scenarios and introduce content-specific diversity measures' referring to lexical diversity metrics based on n-gram statistics from this and related works.

key_contribution: Controlled experiment demonstrating that co-writing with RLHF-tuned LLMs (InstructGPT) significantly increases essay homogenization and reduces both lexical and content diversity compared to solo writing or base LLM (GPT3) assistance, with the effect attributable to the model's less diverse text contributions rather than changes in user writing behavior.
limitations: The study uses now-deprecated OpenAI models (davinci, text-davinci-003) with 38 Upwork participants on a single essay-writing task, so it remains unclear whether the RLHF-diversity tradeoff generalizes to modern instruction-tuned models, other user populations, or longer-term repeated interactions. The interface only provides text continuations, and it is unknown whether richer interaction forms or prompt engineering could mitigate the homogenization effect.
surprise_factor: The asymmetry between GPT3 and InstructGPT is the main conceptual surprise: despite nearly identical usage statistics (acceptance rate ~70%, model-written fraction ~33-35%), only the RLHF-tuned model causes significant homogenization, isolating the fine-tuning process rather than model assistance per se as the diversity-reducing factor. However, effect sizes are modest (e.g., 0.154 vs 0.166 Rouge-L homogenization) and the evidence rests on a single experiment with 38 writers using now-deprecated models, tempering the strength of the claim.

key_contribution: Proposes a Spectral Transformation (ST) framework that generalizes whitening loss for preventing dimensional collapse in self-supervised learning, and introduces INTL (IterNorm with trace loss) as a new ST instance that theoretically guarantees equal-eigenvalue spectrum modulation and achieves state-of-the-art performance on ImageNet classification and COCO detection with small batch sizes.
limitations: The method is primarily validated on CNN backbones (ResNet-18/50) within joint embedding architectures, with ViT results relegated to the appendix; the trace loss coefficient β is empirically regressed from batch size rather than derived theoretically, and the ST framework's applicability to other SSL paradigms (e.g., masked image modeling) remains unexplored.
surprise_factor: The most notable finding is a negative-result surprise: IterNorm, which successfully approximates whitening in supervised learning, unexpectedly suffers severe dimensional collapse and numerical divergence (NAN losses at T≥11) when applied to SSL, contradicting the intuition that a better whitening approximation should transfer directly. The conceptual observation that a narrow band of power exponents (p ∈ [0.45, 0.55]) all prevent collapse, rather than whitening being uniquely special, is a mild but clean conceptual surprise. Overall, the performance gains over SOTA are modest and the contribution is more framework-driven than result-driven.

title: Context is Environment
input: context sequence of unlabeled images from same environment
task_novelty_note: Domain generalization (predicting well on unseen environments) is a well-established task; ICRM is a new method for it.

compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 2 as ARM baseline with average and worst-case OOD test accuracy across all four datasets and context lengths

key_contribution: Proposes In-Context Risk Minimization (ICRM), which reframes domain generalization as in-context prediction by treating the test environment as a sequence of unlabeled examples, proving that attention over this context allows the model to dynamically zoom-in on the test environment risk minimizer and that context-based training itself improves the learned featurizer (outperforming ERM even at zero test-time context).
limitations: The method requires test data to arrive from the same or slowly changing environment, and the OOD theoretical guarantees depend on the test environment falling within the Voronoi cells of training environments. The authors explicitly flag the need to prevent ICRM from zooming in on toxic spurious correlations and identify extending to scenarios with naturally occurring subpopulations or time-based shifts without clear domain separation as future work.
surprise_factor: The most notable finding is that ICRM outperforms ERM even at zero test-time context on WILDS Camelyon17 (92.0% vs 68.6%) and Tiny ImageNet-C (38.3% vs 31.8%), suggesting the context-based training procedure itself yields a better featurizer—a result that goes beyond the straightforward 'more context helps' narrative. The conceptual reframing of invariance (extending the feature space with context reveals invariances that ERM on the raw feature space misses) is elegant but not deeply surprising to those familiar with representation learning. The performance gains with context, while consistent across datasets, are moderate in magnitude and the theoretical guarantees rely on strong assumptions (iid sampling, existence of an ideal amortization function, Voronoi cell containment).

limitations: The generation evaluation is limited to class-conditional benchmarks (ImageNet, Kinetics, UCF-101) rather than the more practically relevant text-to-image/video setting, which the authors explicitly note is out of scope and still under development. The video compression study uses only 30 videos, and the authors acknowledge that further research is needed to adapt the model for efficient CPU inference comparable to standard codecs.
surprise_factor: The conceptual surprise is that a simple sign-based quantization (LFQ) enables a 262K vocabulary that *improves* LM generation quality, directly contradicting the field's working assumption that larger VQ codebooks hurt generation (as shown by the orange curve in Fig. 1). The LM-beats-diffusion result on ImageNet (FID 1.91 vs. 2.65 with guidance at 512×512) is the first such evidence, though the comparison against 2B-parameter diffusion baselines with a 307M MLM makes the 'comparable model size' claim somewhat generous; the fairest comparison (vs. RIN at 320M) shows a smaller gap.

title: Evaluating Language Model Agency Through Negotiations
task_novelty_note: Extends static, single-turn LM evaluation to dynamic, multi-turn, cross-model negotiation-based assessment of agency.

builds_on.title: Rio copa: A negotiation simulation
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'The following negotiation rules are adapted from Bontempo & Iyengar (2008)' in Appendix E.1, directly deriving the game structure and rules from this work

compares_to.title: Gpt-4 technical report
compares_to.evidence: gpt-4 and gpt-3.5 appear in all main results tables (Tables 1-4, 11-14) as models evaluated alongside other LMs in self-play and cross-play negotiation experiments

key_contribution: Introduces a dynamic, co-evolving benchmark for evaluating language model agency through structured multi-turn negotiation games (self-play and cross-play), jointly measuring alignment (faithfulness, instruction-following) and performance (agreement rates, normalized payoffs), revealing that only closed-source models could complete the tasks and that the most powerful model (gpt-4) paradoxically underperformed weaker opponents in negotiation outcomes despite superior faithfulness scores.
limitations: Cost constraints limited the number of experiments (gpt-4 had ~15 runs vs. 25+ for others), and the authors acknowledge that model-specific prompt engineering could further improve results but was not systematically explored. The framework is also limited to a small set of publicly available models at the time of writing, and the authors note that malicious actors could misuse the framework to select only for negotiation ability.
surprise_factor: The most notable finding is a conceptual surprise: GPT-4, despite achieving the highest faithfulness and instruction-following scores, had the lowest self-play agreement rate and required the most rounds to converge, suggesting that raw model capability does not translate to effective negotiation strategy. This is supported by consistent results across multiple game types, though GPT-4 had fewer runs (~15 vs. 25+) due to cost constraints, slightly weakening the evidence.

key_contribution: Introduces the dance accompaniment task with the DD100 duet dance dataset (117 min, 10 genres, 5 professional pairs) and Duolando, a GPT-based follower motion generator enhanced with off-policy reinforcement learning to robustly handle out-of-distribution leader motions and music, establishing a benchmark with interaction-specific metrics (contact frequency, beat echo degree, cross-distance FID).
limitations: The generated follower still lags significantly behind ground truth (FID_k 25.30 vs. 6.56; only ~15% user preference over GT), and the dataset is limited to 5 pairs of professional dancers performing ballroom and ballet genres, restricting generalizability to broader interaction types, dance styles, or performer diversity.
surprise_factor: The most notable finding is the tension between explicit relative translation prediction and motion quality: adding tr prediction collapses FID_cd from 7970 to 21.68 (a 365× improvement) but simultaneously worsens FID_k by 71%, revealing that positional coordination and kinematic plausibility are in direct conflict without the RL correction. The off-policy RL then resolves this by reducing skating ratio by 69%, but the overall gap to ground truth remains large, so the surprise is more diagnostic than transformative.

key_contribution: Demonstrates that combining object-centric slot attention (SA-MESH) with sparse-perturbation causal representation learning resolves the non-injectivity failure of standard disentanglement methods in multi-object scenes, achieving provable k-fold reduction in required perturbations and near-perfect property disentanglement on 2D and 3D synthetic benchmarks.
limitations: Experiments are limited to simple synthetic scenes with only 2–4 objects on homogeneous backgrounds, with no complex dynamics or real-world textures; the authors note that scaling to scenes with many objects, complex backgrounds, and temporal dynamics remains open, and that training SA-MESH from scratch for each configuration is computationally expensive (~12 hours per run on a single A100 GPU).
surprise_factor: The conceptual surprise is that the injectivity assumption, which underpins every identifiability-guaranteeing disentanglement method, is violated by the mere presence of interchangeable objects, capping performance at 1/k — a failure mode that is easy to overlook but fundamental. The k-fold perturbation reduction is a clean theoretical result, though not dramatically surprising given the shared-property structure. Evidence is solid (multiple seeds, 2D and 3D, multiple property combinations) but confined to very simple synthetic scenes, tempering the practical impact.

key_contribution: FedAU, a lightweight extension of FedAvg that adaptively weights client updates using online estimates of participation intervals (with a cutoff parameter K controlling a bias-variance tradeoff), providing the first provable convergence guarantee for federated averaging under unknown, heterogeneous, and uncontrollable client participation statistics at the same O(1) per-client memory cost as vanilla FedAvg.
limitations: The theoretical convergence analysis (Assumption 4) requires time-independent Bernoulli participation across rounds, while Markovian and cyclic patterns are only validated empirically; additionally, the proof requires either a bounded global gradient or a nearly-optimal-weights assumption (Assumption 5). The authors note that extending the analysis to general time-dependent participation processes and incorporating adaptive weighting into other FL algorithm families (e.g., SCAFFOLD) remains open.
surprise_factor: The most notable finding is that FedAU empirically outperforms the idealized 'known participation statistics' baseline, which the authors attribute to the empirical participation path capturing actual client behavior more faithfully than the model-based 1/p_n weight when p_n is very small (e.g., 0.02). This is a mild conceptual surprise — one would expect knowing the true distribution to be strictly better — but the explanation (high variance of empirical counts at low p_n) is reasonable and the effect is modest in magnitude.

key_contribution: Demonstrates that a single frozen transformer block from a pretrained LLM (e.g., LLaMA-7B) inserted as a visual encoder layer consistently improves performance across diverse visual tasks (2D/3D classification, video, motion forecasting, vision-language), and proposes the information filtering hypothesis explaining that the LLM block identifies and amplifies informative visual tokens.
limitations: The paper explicitly notes that experiments prioritize task diversity over state-of-the-art performance due to computational constraints, and that the information filtering hypothesis does not yet explain how training dynamics facilitate cooperation between visual features and the frozen language transformer, nor how to quantify the distinct functions of individual LLM layers.
surprise_factor: The conceptual surprise is genuine and well-evidenced: a transformer block that has never seen visual input, trained exclusively on text, improves visual encoding when frozen and inserted into diverse visual pipelines (images, point clouds, video, trajectories). The breadth across six task types, two LLM families (LLaMA, OPT), and the ablation showing the effect is not merely increased capacity (MLP control) or random initialization (random LLM control) makes this a robust finding. However, the practical magnitude is modest (sub-2% gains), and the information filtering hypothesis, while intuitive, remains qualitative and does not yet explain the training dynamics or per-layer roles.

title: Skeleton-of-Thought: Prompting LLMs for Efficient Parallel Generation
task_novelty_note: Reducing LLM inference latency is a well-established task; SoT contributes a new prompting-based method rather than a new problem formulation.
key_contribution: Proposes Skeleton-of-Thought (SoT), a two-stage prompting technique that guides LLMs to first generate a concise answer skeleton and then expand each point in parallel via batched decoding or parallel API calls, achieving up to 2.39× end-to-end speed-up on 8 of 12 LLMs while maintaining or improving answer quality on several question categories, establishing a novel data-level pathway for inference efficiency.
limitations: SoT is fundamentally unsuitable for questions requiring step-by-step reasoning (e.g., math, coding) where later steps depend on earlier ones, and the acceleration ratio is less predictable and controllable than model- or system-level techniques since it depends on the prompt, model, and question. Additionally, for API-based models, SoT increases prefilling token overhead and thus cost, and in saturated serving scenarios it may hurt throughput due to parallel requests.
surprise_factor: The main conceptual surprise is that a simple two-stage prompt (generate skeleton → expand points in parallel) achieves meaningful end-to-end speed-ups on off-the-shelf LLMs with zero model modification, challenging the near-universal assumption that autoregressive sequential decoding is the only viable inference mode. However, the speed-ups are modest (1.5–2.4×), quality gains are inconsistent across categories, and the method clearly fails on reasoning-heavy questions, so the practical surprise is tempered.

key_contribution: First demonstration that Probabilistic Circuits (a class of Tractable Probabilistic Models) can exactly and efficiently compute the constrained posterior to steer the denoising process of diffusion models, producing more semantically coherent inpainted images with only ~10% additional computational overhead across three high-resolution datasets.
limitations: The PC operates in a VQ-GAN latent space rather than directly on pixels, losing full tractability over individual pixels and requiring Monte Carlo approximation (4–8 samples) for the latent-space soft-evidence computation. The authors note that directly modeling high-resolution (256×256) pixel-space data with PCs remains an open gap, and the empirical gains over the strongest baseline (CoPaint) are modest, with Tiramisu losing on 3 out of 21 settings.
surprise_factor: The conceptual surprise is moderate: the idea that a relatively simple tractable model (a PC) can usefully steer a far more expressive intractable model (a diffusion model) to produce better inpaintings is counterintuitive and challenges the assumption that only the most expressive model should drive generation. However, the empirical gains are modest (small LPIPS improvements over CoPaint, with a few losses), and the approach requires a separately trained PC plus VQ-GAN, so the practical 'surprise' is tempered by the engineering overhead and limited margins.

key_contribution: Proves a unified W₂-distance discretization error bound O(η^θ + η^{θ/2+γ/4}) between a general class of Ito chains (subsuming Langevin dynamics, SGD, and boosting) and their corresponding Ito diffusions, under the broadest assumptions to date: arbitrary non-Gaussian state-dependent noise, no convexity, and no dissipativity, via a novel window coupling technique and a non-Markovian Girsanov theorem.
limitations: The exponential dependence on the time horizon T limits applicability for sampling from invariant measures, and the uniform ellipticity requirement on the diffusion coefficient σ (strictly non-singular with eigenvalues bounded away from zero) remains a restriction compared to degenerate-diffusion analyses such as Li et al. (2019a).
surprise_factor: The conceptual surprise is that a simple 'window coupling' regularization term (analogous to L₂-regularization) is sufficient to replace the structural dissipativity/convexity assumptions that prior work relied on, enabling W₂ bounds in the fully non-dissipative regime. The improvement from O(η^{1/8}) to O(η^{3/4}) for SGD is substantial, though it comes with the trade-off of exponential horizon dependence.

title: On the Generalization Capacity of Neural Networks During Generic Multimodal Reasoning
task_novelty_note: Extends compositional generalization evaluation from single-modality, fixed-depth (≤3) task trees to multimodal, arbitrarily deep task trees with explicit OOD distractor splits.

builds_on.title: A Dataset and Architecture for Visual Reasoning with a Working Memory
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'gCOG is a configurable question-answer dataset, originally inspired from COG (Yang et al., 2018)' and 'We adapted the previously-developed COG task' with specific modifications to operators, categorical tokens, and task tree depth.

builds_on.title: Perceiver: General Perception with Iterative Attention
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'we included a Perceiver-like model (Jaegle et al., 2021), an architecture designed to generically process multimodal inputs' and directly implements its latent Transformer with cross-attention structure.

key_contribution: Introduction of gCOG, a configurable multimodal compositional generalization benchmark with explicit OOD splits for distractor, systematic, and productive generalization, and a comprehensive evaluation showing that cross-attention mechanisms between modalities are necessary for strong distractor and systematic generalization, while no tested architecture (including scaled BERT-style models) achieves productive compositional generalization.
limitations: All evaluations use modality-agnostic categorical tokens rather than actual images or natural language, so findings may not directly transfer to modality-specific domains. The task is constrained to binary tree structures and encoder-only architectures, and the productive generalization failure, while consistent across all models, is demonstrated on a single synthetic task family, leaving open whether the limitation is specific to the binary-tree formulation or truly fundamental to current neural architectures.
surprise_factor: The most notable finding is a negative-result surprise: every architecture tested — including cross-attention models that excel at distractor and systematic generalization — completely fails on productive compositional generalization, and scaling to BERT-small size provides zero improvement. This is somewhat consistent with prior Transformer compositionality failures (Dziri et al., 2023), but the systematic demonstration across six architectures with controlled training makes the architectural limitation more concrete and actionable.
